Mechanism-guided protease-based strategies for foodborne biofilm control: From EPS protein targets to green delivery systems
abstract: Background Foodborne bacterial biofilms formed on food-contact surfaces and processing equipment are persistent contamination reservoirs because their resistance to sanitation is strongly linked to the chemically diverse and spatially heterogeneous extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix. Proteinaceous EPS components, including adhesins, amyloid fibers, scaffold proteins, and surface-associated assemblies, play key roles in adhesion, cohesion, matrix mechanics, and adaptive remodeling. Scope and approach This review examines the protein-centered architecture and stage-dependent remodeling of foodborne biofilms and evaluates proteases as functional interfacial tools for disrupting proteinaceous EPS networks. It integrates evidence on protease targets and functional modes, environmental and food-matrix constraints, green encapsulation and plant-based delivery systems, protease–essential oil co-delivery, and molecular and thermodynamic determinants of protease–EPS interactions. Key findings and conclusions Protease efficacy depends not only on catalytic activity but also on target identity, substrate accessibility, matrix organization, environmental conditions, and interfacial binding. Proteases can limit surface anchoring, dismantle structural scaffolds, decouple composite EPS networks, and promote dispersal-oriented matrix weakening, particularly when combined with complementary antimicrobial treatments. Green delivery systems can improve enzyme stability, regulate release, and enhance access to EPS substrates, while protease–essential oil co-delivery couples matrix disruption with microbial killing and suppression of regrowth. Overall, a mechanism-guided framework integrating EPS protein mapping, protease–substrate interactions, carrier design, and validation on food-contact surfaces offers a promising route toward precision biofilm control in food systems. Molecular modeling and thermodynamic analyses are positioned as complementary tools for mechanistic interpretation and hypothesis testing.

The clean-label paradigm: innovative ingredients and emerging technologies for reduced-phosphate meat formulations
abstract: There is a growing trend for clean-label food products, characterized by a reduced use of synthetic additives. In this context, processed meat products have drawn particular attention, as they typically contain phosphates that enhance several sensory and technological characteristics of the food. This review aimed to evaluate the next generation strategies in meat products. The findings indicate that these strategies can be divided into four main categories: (i) natural ingredients, (ii) emerging technologies, (iii) chemical alternatives, and (iv) co-products and by-products from industry. Natural ingredients (e.g., vegetables and mushrooms), rich in fibers and phenolic compounds, were shown to improve water-holding capacity, strengthen the three-dimensional protein network, and enhance oxidative stability. The emerging technologies (e.g., ultrasound, high pressure processing, and pulsed electric field) showed considerable potential for application in clean-label products by inducing conformational changes in protein structures and conferring greater stability to meat emulsions. Alkaline carbonates, bicarbonate, and chloride-based salts are recognized as alternatives that exhibit similar mechanisms of action to phosphate. Co-products and by-products were considered functional ingredients, allowing the clean-label demand to be aligned with the demand for more sustainable production systems. Several challenges remain for the development of these meat products, including significant sensory changes, microbiological stability, and higher production costs. Since no single alternative replaces all phosphate functions, future studies should combine functional ingredients and emerging technologies and evaluate long-term oxidative stability, microbiological safety, and sensory acceptance.
